prompt.context: An investment company has purchased a 12th-century chateau in central France, located about 3.5 hours from Paris and 1 hour from the Loire Valley. The local area is primarily countryside and small villages with lots of tourist attractions within a 1-hour drive. The castle has been unused for roughly 30 years, but once refurbished it will operate as a 6-bedroom bed and breakfast. The company is looking for 50 investors to pay $15,000 each to start up the business. Each investor will receive 2 weeks per year of free stay at the castle as well as a 1% ownership stake in the company. You have been out of college for a few years and have managed to save some money.
prompt.question: How would you go about considering whether or not to invest?

clarifying_info.q: What is the total initial investment required?
clarifying_info.a: $1M purchase price + $250K renovations + $250K furnishings = $1.5M total. The 50 investors contribute $750K; the remaining $750K comes from a bank loan.

clarifying_info.q: What is the interest rate on the debt?
clarifying_info.a: 10% per year on the $750K bank loan, so $75K in annual interest.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major operating costs?
clarifying_info.a: Interest on debt $75K, proprietor salary $40K, landscaping $10K, laundry service $10K, marketing $10K, breakfast food $10K, utilities $5K, miscellaneous $15K — total $175K per year. (Note: 400 days/year is used to simplify the math.)
5 guests x 400 days = 2,000 breakfasts x $5 cost each = $10K.
Local countryside B&Bs charge $50–$125/night; castle B&Bs elsewhere in France charge $300–$500/night; upscale Paris hotels charge $400–$500/night.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average regional occupancy rate?
clarifying_info.a: Local tourist offices report 50% average occupancy, confirmed by key competitors.

framework: Frame the investment decision as a profitability / break-even analysis of the chateau business
Estimate total initial investment and funding structure (equity vs. debt)
Identify all annual operating cost buckets (fixed vs. variable)
Estimate annual revenue potential: price per night x occupancy x available room-nights
Adjust available room-nights for investor stay entitlements
Calculate break-even occupancy and compare to regional benchmark
Assess key risks: occupancy/demand, execution, exit liquidity
Synthesize: does the business make money, and would you personally invest?

questions.prompt: Estimate the chateau's financials. Will it make money?
questions.guidance: Candidate should break the problem into (1) initial investment, (2) annual costs, (3) annual revenue, then compute break-even occupancy. Strong answers note that investor weeks reduce sellable inventory and that 50% occupancy matches the regional benchmark — making the investment appear viable. Superior answers also question which 50% matters (rooms vs. total nights) and surface the $140K cost of investor weeks foregone.

math.setup: Annual cost base vs. revenue at various occupancy levels; break-even occupancy calculation
steps: Funding: 50 investors x $15K = $750K equity; $750K bank debt
Gross room-night capacity: 6 rooms x 400 nights = 2,400 room-nights
Revenue at 100% occupancy (before investor adjustment): 2,400 x $200 = $480K
Revenue at 50% occupancy (before investor adjustment): $480K x 50% = $240K — covers $175K costs, so profitable
Investor entitlement cost: 50 investors x 2 weeks x $1,400/week = $140K foregone revenue
Adjusted revenue at 50% occupancy: $340K x 50% = $170K — below $175K annual costs, nearly break-even
At ~52% occupancy on adjusted inventory the chateau breaks even
math.answer: At a $200/night price and 50% occupancy the chateau generates ~$170K in adjusted revenue against $175K in costs — roughly at break-even. Any occupancy above ~52% (on sellable nights) yields profit. Given regional average occupancy of 50%, the investment is marginal but plausible.

questions.prompt: What are the key risks to this investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify occupancy risk (small marketing budget, remote location), execution risk (French contractor delays, budget overruns), and exit/liquidity risk (hard to find a buyer if the business fails). Strong candidates connect the tiny $10K marketing budget to the occupancy risk directly.

questions.prompt: Suppose the company is returning over $100K profit per year. What should it consider doing next?
questions.guidance: Candidate should discuss: paying down existing bank debt to reduce $75K interest burden; identifying additional revenue streams at the current castle (events, wine tours, etc.); expanding by acquiring new castles. For new-castle prioritization, strong answers address size (larger castles have better unit economics), geography (proximity to existing contractors and local knowledge), and target customer overlap.

questions.prompt: Would you invest? What else would you want to know?
questions.guidance: Candidate should synthesize the profitability analysis with personal risk tolerance and frame additional diligence needs: management team quality, track record of similar investments in France or elsewhere, customer survey data on willingness to pay $200/night, a detailed marketing plan, legal structure of the 1% stake, and exit provisions.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should an investor consider before committing $15K to this venture?

categories.name: Demand / Occupancy Risk
ideas: Tiny $10K annual marketing budget limits awareness
Remote location 3.5 hours from Paris — difficult for weekend travelers
Unclear target customer and booking channel strategy
Seasonality: tourist demand concentrated in summer months
Competition from established Loire Valley B&Bs

categories.name: Execution Risk
ideas: Renovation and furnishing budget overruns possible
Finding and retaining a qualified proprietor at $40K salary
Unexpected capital expenditure after opening (repairs, upgrades)

categories.name: Financial / Structural Risk
ideas: Break-even occupancy is close to regional average — no margin of safety
$750K bank debt at 10% creates fixed $75K annual obligation
Investor weeks reduce sellable inventory, compressing revenue potential
No stated dividend or cash return mechanism beyond free stays

categories.name: Exit / Liquidity Risk
ideas: Hard to find a buyer for a 1% stake in an illiquid private chateau business
No clear exit timeline or buyout mechanism
Property value in remote French countryside may appreciate slowly
If chateau fails, $15K investment is largely unrecoverable

recommendation: The chateau is roughly at break-even at regional average occupancy (50%), with profitability dependent on achieving occupancy slightly above that benchmark
The $15K investment is speculative but provides tangible value through 2 weeks of annual free stay (worth ~$1,400/week at $200/night) in addition to the 1% equity stake
risks: Occupancy may not reach 50% given the small marketing budget and remote location
Renovation costs and contractor delays could erode the initial capital before the chateau opens
The equity stake is illiquid — there is no guaranteed exit or buyout mechanism
Investor stay entitlements reduce sellable inventory, making the economics tighter than a simple 50%-occupancy headline suggests
next_steps: Conduct primary research: survey potential guests on willingness to pay $200+/night for a chateau B&B experience
Review management team credentials and any comparable investments they have executed
Obtain a detailed marketing plan explaining how $10K will drive sufficient occupancy
Model downside scenario (30–40% occupancy) to understand maximum loss exposure
Review legal documents governing the 1% stake, investor rights, and exit provisions
